Depends. I don't believe there are any regulations preventing the average Joe from entering into an agreement with a backbone carrier. Granted, the agreement itself tends to be more expensive on a monthly basis compared to your average consumer net connection, but in terms of providing high throughput WAN connectivity, it's hard to beat.

So you would have citizens entering into a collective cost sharing project to create the mesh network and split the cost of the backbone WAN connection that they need in order to reach the wider internet.

You still have the whole private company holding a lot of cards, but backbone carriers were never the ones pushing for fast lanes and similar bullshit-- that was always the last-mile carriers.

I do have to burst the bubble a bit here on the whole mesh network dream though. Unless people plan on creating massive networks of ethernet and connect the entire place on a LAN, your options are really limited. Firstly, a fact that most don't realize about wifi is that it is half duplex. Presented with this fact most can figure out why-- there's only one electromagnetic spectrum, therefor only one device can broadcast on a given channel within that spectrum within its range or else collisions happen.

A corollary to that is that throughput in a mesh network decreases by 50% for each wireless hop required between the client and the nearest WAN connection. This is due to the fact that the number of transmissions required increase linearly (and therefor in the best cast, bandwidth decreases by 1/n for n number of hops). Add in the increased network communication and the resulting increase in cross-talk and you arrive at the 50% rule-of-thumb.

So there is a mathematical giant middle finger hiding in mesh networks and there isn't really an innovative way around it.

I support repealing net neutrality as it exists right now. I do not believe the internet is a utility or a right. I do believe that ISP's should have the ability to provide faster or slower content, data caps, or refuse to load sites. I would require some changes from ISP's however.

  • Infrastructure should be maintained by all ISP's up to a common standard using a flat tax against revenue
  • Every region above a certain population level should have at least 4 providers to choose from
  • Small or difficult to reach regions should receive incentives to ensure quality access
